goals: Write and trace if, if-else, if-else-if ladder and nested if statements
Predict the pairing of an else in nested if statements
Find the effect of a stray semicolon and of = used in place of ==
Write slab-based programs such as bills and grades with an if-else-if ladder

slides.heading: if constructs
slides.body_md: Part 1: **if**, **if-else**, the **if-else-if ladder**, **nested if**, the **dangling else** and the commonest mistakes.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: if, if-else, if-else-if ladder, nested if, dangling else and common mistakes
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Welcome to the revision of conditional constructs. In this part we revise the if statement, if else, the else if ladder and nested if. We trace programs step by step and study the dangling else. Then we learn to spot two common mistakes: a semicolon after the condition, and a single equals sign where a double equals sign was meant. A short note on comparing strings finishes the part.

slides.heading: Making decisions
slides.body_md: A **selection statement** chooses which statements to execute, depending on a **condition**: an expression that is either true or false. In Java the condition must have the type **boolean**.

rows: run a block only when a condition is true
choose one block out of several alternatives, testing in order
take a second decision only after the first one

visual.alt: Table of the four conditional constructs: if has one branch, if-else has two, the if-else-if ladder has three or more and nested if places a decision inside another

slides.narration: A selection statement chooses which statements will run, depending on a condition. A condition is an expression that is either true or false, and in Java it must be of the boolean type. The table lists the four constructs of this chapter. The plain if has one branch, if else has two, a ladder has three or more, and a nested if places one decision inside another.

slides.heading: The if statement

visual.alt: Table of two runs of the if statement: temp 39 makes the condition true and prints Fever; temp 36 makes it false and prints nothing
visual.caption: When the condition is false, the statement is simply skipped.

slides.narration: The if statement runs a statement only when its condition is true. In the program, a temperature of thirty nine makes the condition true, so the word Fever is printed. A temperature of thirty six makes the condition false, and the statement is simply skipped. Nothing is printed, because there is no else part to run instead.

slides.heading: if-else: two branches
slides.body_md: In an **if-else** statement exactly one of two blocks runs: the if block when the condition is true, the else block when it is false.

slides.heading: Braces and the single statement

rows: only the first statement after the condition

visual.alt: Table comparing an if without braces, which controls only one statement and prints Checked, with an if with braces, which controls both statements and prints nothing when the condition is false
visual.caption: Indentation does not matter to Java; braces do.

slides.narration: Without braces, an if controls only the single statement that follows it. In the first program the condition is false, so the line Large is skipped, but the next line is outside the if, so it is printed. Its indentation does not matter to Java. When two or more statements belong to the if, put them inside braces, as in the second version, and neither is printed.

slides.narration: Use a ladder when there are three or more alternatives. The conditions are tested one after another from the top. The first true condition runs its block, and then control leaves the ladder at once. The remaining conditions are never tested. If none is true, the final else block runs. Because the order of tests matters, the strictest limit usually has to come first.

slides.heading: The dangling else
slides.body_md: When an else follows nested ifs without braces, Java pairs it with the **nearest unmatched if**, whatever the indentation suggests. Braces can change the pairing.

rows: indented under the first if, no braces

visual.alt: Table of the dangling else: without braces the else belongs to the inner if and the program prints Retail / Done; with braces closing the inner if, the else belongs to the first if and the program prints Done
visual.caption: Java pairs an else with the nearest unmatched if, whatever the indentation shows.

slides.narration: This is the dangling else. In the first program the else is indented under the first if, but Java pairs it with the nearest unmatched if, the one that tests the order. So the program prints Retail, and then Done. In the second program the inner if is closed by braces, the else now belongs to the first if, and only Done is printed.

slides.heading: Quick check: which if gets the else?
slides.body_md: Write the exact output.
slides.narration: Ignore the indentation and pair the else with the nearest unmatched if.

slides.heading: Mistake 1: a semicolon after the condition

visual.alt: Table of the stray semicolon: with the semicolon the word Pass is printed for marks 28 and for 45; without it the word is printed only for 45
visual.caption: A semicolon after the condition makes an empty statement the body of the if.

slides.narration: A semicolon directly after the condition is the first common mistake. It forms an empty statement, and that empty statement becomes the whole body of the if. The statement on the next line is then outside the if and always runs. With marks twenty eight the word Pass is printed, which is wrong. The compiler does not complain, so such a logical error must be found by tracing.

slides.heading: Mistake 2: = instead of ==
slides.body_md: A single **=** assigns; **==** compares. With an int the compiler rejects the condition; with a boolean variable it is accepted and gives a wrong result.

rows: compile-time error: incompatible types: int cannot be converted to boolean

visual.alt: Table of the equals sign mistake: with an int, the single equals sign gives the compile-time error incompatible types: int cannot be converted to boolean; with a boolean variable it compiles and prints Open, a logical error; the double equals sign compares correctly

slides.narration: The second mistake uses a single equals sign where a double one was needed. With an int variable, the assignment gives an int, and an if needs a boolean, so the compiler reports an error. With a boolean variable, the assignment is accepted, the variable is changed to true, and the if branch always runs. The correct comparison uses the double equals sign.

slides.heading: Quick check: braces
slides.body_md: Choose the correct output.
slides.narration: Remember which statement is controlled by an if that has no braces.

slides.heading: Conditions with logical operators
slides.body_md: Join tests with **&&**, **||** and **!** to make one condition. **&&** is evaluated before **||**. Strings are compared with `equals`, not `==` (see Chapter 13).

visual.alt: Table of the values of five conditions: a > 0 && b > 0 is false; a > 0 || b > 0 is true; !(a > 5) is false; a < 0 && b > 0 || c > 0 is true; "Delhi".equals("Delhi") is true
visual.caption: Strings are compared with equals, not ==. Chapter 13 studies Strings in detail.

slides.narration: Several tests can be joined into one condition with the logical and, the logical or and the logical not. The logical and is evaluated before the logical or, so brackets are useful for clarity. The last row of the table compares two strings. Strings are compared with the equals method and not with the double equals operator. We study strings fully in a later chapter.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: condition must be boolean; braces for more than one statement
conditions tested from the top; first true one wins; order matters
inner test made only after the outer one
else pairs with the nearest unmatched if

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: boolean conditions and braces, ladder order, nested if, the dangling else, the stray semicolon and the difference between assignment and comparison

slides.narration: To sum up Part 1. A condition must be a boolean expression, and braces are needed for more than one controlled statement. A ladder tests from the top and the first true condition wins, so the order matters. A nested if makes the inner test only after the outer one. An else pairs with the nearest unmatched if. A semicolon after the condition is a logical error, and assignment is not comparison.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: In a ladder write the conditions in the right order: the largest limit first.
Trace the program with the given values; write each condition as true or false.
Ignore indentation when you pair an else: it belongs to the nearest unmatched `if`.
Check for a stray `;` after `if (...)` and for `=` written in place of `==`.
In a program, validate the input first (for example marks outside 0 to 100) and use `&&` and `||` carefully.
slides.narration: Some exam tips. Write the conditions of a ladder in the right order, with the largest limit first. Trace each program with the given values and note whether every condition is true or false. Ignore the indentation when pairing an else. Look for a stray semicolon after a condition and for a single equals sign used for comparison. In a program, check the validity of the input first.

goals: Write and trace switch statements on int, char and String selectors
Predict the output of a switch with and without break, including fall-through
Convert between switch and if-else-if constructs where possible
Write a menu-driven program using switch and end it with System.exit(0)

slides.heading: switch and menu-driven programs
slides.body_md: Part 2: the **switch** statement, **break** and **default**, **fall-through**, **menu-driven programs** and **System.exit(0)**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: switch syntax, break and default, fall-through, rules for case labels, switch or ladder, menu-driven programs and System.exit(0)
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: Welcome to the second part. We study the switch statement with its case labels, break and default. We see what happens when a break is missing, which is called fall through, and when it is useful. We compare switch with the else if ladder, write menu driven programs with a switch on the choice, and finally see how the exit method ends a program early.

slides.heading: The switch statement

rows: the expression whose value is compared; int, char or String
a label with a constant; runs when selector equals it
runs when no case matches; optional

visual.alt: Table of the parts of a switch statement: the selector, case labels with constants, break, default and the braces

slides.narration: A switch statement compares one value, called the selector, with a list of constants. Each constant is written after the word case and a colon. The matching case runs. The word break leaves the switch. The word default marks the statements that run when nothing matches, and it is optional. All the cases sit inside one pair of braces.

slides.heading: What can be the selector?
slides.body_md: The selector may be an **int** (or byte, short), a **char** or a **String**. A real number, a long or a boolean is not allowed.

rows: selector type double is not allowed
selector type long is not allowed
selector type boolean is not allowed

visual.alt: Table of selector types: int, char and String are accepted; double, long and boolean are rejected with the messages selector type double is not allowed, selector type long is not allowed and selector type boolean is not allowed

slides.narration: The selector of a switch can be an int, a char or a String. Strings were allowed from Java seven. Real numbers, long values and booleans are rejected by the compiler, and the table shows the messages. When a string is the selector, the match is exact, so capital and small letters are different.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: the day name

visual.alt: Trace table of the day program: day 2 prints Tuesday; day 3 prints Wednesday; day 7 prints Other day

slides.narration: Let us trace the day program. Day two matches the label two, prints Tuesday, and the break leaves the switch. Day three matches the label three and prints Wednesday. Day seven matches no label, so the default statement runs and the program prints Other day. The default needs no break, because it is the last part of the switch.

slides.heading: break and default
slides.body_md: When the selector matches a case, its statements run until a **break** is reached; **break** then leaves the switch. **default** runs only when no case matches.

visual.alt: Flow of a switch with break: the selector is evaluated, the matching case is found, its statements run, break is reached and control leaves the switch
visual.caption: With break, only the matching case runs.

slides.narration: This flow shows a switch with break. The selector is evaluated first. Then the matching case is found, and its statements run. When the break is reached, control leaves the switch, and the program continues with the statement after the closing brace. Because of the break, only the matching case runs. The default part is used when no case matches.

slides.heading: Fall-through
slides.body_md: If a case has **no break**, execution **falls through** into the next case and continues until a break or the end of the switch.

slides.heading: Rules for case labels
slides.body_md: Each case label must be a **constant**, must be **unique** in the switch and must have a type suitable for the selector. A **final** variable with a constant value is also accepted.

rows: Label type must suit the selector
incompatible types: String cannot be converted to int

visual.alt: Table of the rules for case labels and the compiler messages when each is broken: constant expression required; duplicate case label; incompatible types: String cannot be converted to int
visual.caption: A final variable with a constant value is accepted as a label.

slides.narration: There are rules for case labels. A label must be a constant and not an ordinary variable. Each label must be unique inside one switch. The type of the label must suit the selector. If a rule is broken, the compiler gives an error, and the table shows the messages. A final variable with a constant value is accepted as a constant.

slides.heading: switch or if-else-if?
slides.body_md: A **switch** tests **equality** with constants; a ladder can test any condition. Use switch for a fixed list of exact values and a ladder for ranges.

rows: equality of one selector with constants
continues into next case unless break
a fixed list of exact values

visual.alt: Comparison table of switch and the if-else-if ladder: what they test, selector type, which branch is taken and what each is best for

slides.narration: How do we choose between the two? A switch tests whether one selector equals a constant, so it suits a list of exact values such as day numbers or menu choices. A ladder can test any condition, including ranges such as marks at least seventy five, and it has no restriction on types. In a switch, the matching case continues into the next unless there is a break.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: converting a ladder to a switch

visual.alt: Table showing that the ladder and the switch print the same text for the grades A, B and Z

slides.narration: Let us convert a ladder into a switch. The ladder tests a grade letter for equality with A and B. Each test becomes a case label with its own break, and the final else becomes default. The table shows that for grades A, B and Z both versions print the same text. A ladder with range conditions could not be converted in this way.

slides.heading: Reading the choice with Scanner
slides.body_md: The way the choice is read decides the type of the selector and of the labels. The Scanner class has no method to read a char directly: read a word and take its first character.

visual.alt: Table of how a menu choice is read with Scanner: nextInt for a number with labels such as case 1; next followed by charAt zero for a letter with labels such as case a; next for a word with labels such as case stop

slides.narration: How the choice is read decides the type of the selector. For a numbered menu, read an int with the next int method and write number labels. For a lettered menu, read a word with the next method and take its first character, because Scanner has no method that reads a single character. For commands in words, read a string and use string labels.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: For output questions, find the matching label first, then run down the cases until a `break`.
If no label matches and there is a `default`, start there; remember that `default` may be written anywhere.
Case labels must be constants and unique; the selector cannot be `double`, `long` or `boolean`.
In a menu-driven program use `break` in every case, and give `default` a message for an invalid choice.
After `System.exit(0)` nothing is executed: do not include later lines in the output.
slides.narration: Some exam tips. In output questions, find the matching label first and then run down the cases until a break. If no label matches, start at default. Case labels must be unique constants, and the selector cannot be a real number, a long or a boolean. In a menu driven program, put a break in every case and give default a message. Nothing runs after the exit call.

notes.title: Conditional Constructs: notes

sections.heading: 1. Selection statements: if and if-else
sections.body_md:
A **selection statement** chooses the statements to execute according to a **condition**, an expression of type boolean.

- **if:** the controlled statement runs only when the condition is true.
- **if-else:** one of two blocks runs.
- Without braces the if (or else) controls only the next single statement; use braces for a block.

```java
if (marks >= 40)
    System.out.println("Pass");
else
    System.out.println("Fail");
```

For marks = 56 the output is `Pass`.

To compare Strings use the method `equals` (not `==`): `"Delhi".equals("Delhi")` gives true.

key_terms.definition_md: A statement that chooses which statements to execute depending on a condition.
An expression of type boolean that is either true or false.
A selection statement that executes a statement or block only when its condition is true.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- A stray `;` after `if (...)`, or `=` where `==` was meant.
- Writing the wider condition first in a ladder.
- Trusting indentation to pair an else.
- Forgetting `break`, so that the next case also runs.
- A variable or a repeated constant used as a case label; a `double`, `long` or `boolean` selector.
- Forgetting `default` in a menu-driven program, so that a wrong choice gives no message.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Output questions: each line in the exact order and format.
- Error questions: the error named and the line given.
- Programs (15 marks): class and method structure, input, logic (conditions in the right order), output, variable description or comments.

questions.stem_md: What is the job of an if statement in a Java program?

options.text_md: It repeats a block of statements a fixed number of times
It executes a statement or a block only when its condition is true
It chooses one block out of many by matching a constant value
It stops the program when an error occurs

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** It executes a statement or a block only when its condition is true. An if statement is a selection (decision-making) statement: the condition is evaluated once and the controlled statement runs only if it is true. Repeating is the work of loops, matching constants is the work of switch, and stopping the program is done by System.exit().

questions.stem_md: The condition written inside the brackets of an if statement must be an expression of which type?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** boolean. Java does not treat numbers as true or false. Using an int variable alone as the condition is rejected by the compiler with the message "incompatible types: int cannot be converted to boolean".

**Correct option: (a)** `10.0`. The conditions of a ladder are tested from the top and only the first true one is used. 3400 is not at least 5000, but it is at least 3000, so discount becomes 10 and the remaining tests are skipped. The other options belong to the bills 5200, 1500, 600.

questions.stem_md: In a program the keyword else follows two nested if statements and no braces are written. Which if does that else belong to?

options.text_md: The first if of the program
The nearest if above it that does not yet have an else
None of them; the compiler reports an error

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The nearest if above it that does not yet have an else. An else always pairs with the closest unmatched if, whatever the indentation suggests. For example, with p = 8 and q = 3 the unbraced program `if (p > 5)     if (q > 5)         System.out.println("alpha");     else         System.out.println("beta");` displays `beta`, because the else belongs to the inner if. Braces can change the pairing.

**Correct option: (c)** `Pass`. The semicolon right after the closing bracket is itself a complete (empty) statement, so it becomes the whole body of the if. The println that follows is an ordinary statement and always runs. 28 is below 33, yet the word appears; this is a logical error and the compiler does not complain.

options.text_md: Compile-time error: incompatible types: int cannot be converted to boolean

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Compile-time error: incompatible types: int cannot be converted to boolean. The expression count = 4 is an assignment, and its value is the int 4. An if needs a boolean, so javac stops with "incompatible types: int cannot be converted to boolean". The comparison operator is the double equals sign.

questions.stem_md: Which statement correctly describes the operators = and == of Java?

options.text_md: = compares two values and gives true or false, while == stores a value in a variable
Both operators compare two values, but == is used only for Strings
Both operators store a value in a variable, but == also displays it
= stores the value on its right in the variable on its left, while == compares two values and gives true or false

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** = stores the value on its right in the variable on its left, while == compares two values and gives true or false. The single equals sign is the assignment operator and the double equals sign is the relational (equality) operator. This is why `if (x = 5)` with an int variable is rejected: the compiler says "incompatible types: int cannot be converted to boolean".

**Correct option: (b)** `Half`. The outer condition marks >= 75 is true, so the inner if is evaluated. There income <= 300000 is false, so the inner else runs. Full would need an income of at most 300000, and None a mark below 75.

questions.stem_md: Which statement about an if-else-if ladder is correct?

options.text_md: The conditions are tested from the top and only the block of the first true condition is executed
All the conditions are tested and the block of every true condition is executed
The conditions are tested from the bottom upwards
The final else is compulsory, otherwise the program does not compile

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The conditions are tested from the top and only the block of the first true condition is executed. Once a condition is true its block runs and the rest of the ladder is skipped. The final else is optional: a ladder without it compiles, and a value that fails every test simply skips the ladder: with bill = 200 and only the tests bill >= 1000 and bill >= 500, the program displays nothing.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following describes a nested if statement?

options.text_md: Two if statements written one after the other
An if statement placed inside the block of another if or else statement
An if statement that is followed by an else part
An if statement whose condition joins two tests with && or ||

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** An if statement placed inside the block of another if or else statement. In a nested if the inner statement is evaluated only when the outer branch is taken, so the second decision depends on the first. Two separate ifs are independent, and && and || only build a longer condition.

**Correct option: (c)** `Yes`. The operator && has higher precedence than ||, so the condition is (a < 0 && b > 0) || (c > 0). The first part is false because a is positive, the second part is true, and false OR true is true. Reading it as a < 0 && (b > 0 || c > 0) would give No.

options.text_md: Large and Checked on two lines

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** `Checked`. Without braces the if controls only the single statement that follows it, so the Large line is skipped. The second println is outside the if, and its indentation does not change that. Writing both statements inside braces would hide both lines when the condition is false.

questions.stem_md: What does the break statement do when it is executed inside a case of a switch statement?

It transfers control out of the switch statement

questions.stem_md: What does the statement System.exit(0); do when it is executed?

options.text_md: It terminates the running program immediately, the value 0 meaning normal termination
It leaves only the switch statement in which it is written
It returns from the current method to the method that called it
It restarts the program from the first statement of main

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** It terminates the running program immediately, the value 0 meaning normal termination. System.exit() ends the whole program (the Java Virtual Machine) at once; it is not limited to the current switch, loop or method. The argument 0 is the conventional status for a normal end.

**Correct option: (d)** `Start / Invalid`. The first println runs. Because 9 is more than 5, the if block prints Invalid and calls System.exit(0), which ends the program on the spot, so the line after the if is never executed. With a choice such as 2 the program would instead print Start and Continue.

questions.stem_md: In a menu-driven program that uses switch on the choice, what is the best use of the default label?

To tell the user that the choice is invalid
To repeat the menu for ever
To read the next value with Scanner

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** To tell the user that the choice is invalid. A choice outside the menu matches no case, so default is the place for a message such as Invalid choice (and, if wished, System.exit(0)). It does not repeat anything by itself.

questions.stem_md: A menu uses the letters a, b and c as choices. Which statement correctly reads the choice typed by the user into a char variable ch, with the Scanner object sc?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** `char ch = sc.next().charAt(0);`. The Scanner class has no method to read a char directly, so a word is read with next() and its first character is taken with charAt(0). The other lines fail: nextChar gives "cannot find symbol", nextLine gives "incompatible types: String cannot be converted to char" and nextInt gives "incompatible types: possible lossy conversion from int to char".

questions.stem_md: What is a menu-driven program?

options.text_md: A program that has methods but no main method
A program that displays a list of options, accepts the choice of the user and performs the task for that choice
A program that prints a table of contents of its own code
A program that can be run only from the menu bar of BlueJ

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** A program that displays a list of options, accepts the choice of the user and performs the task for that choice. A menu-driven program lets the user choose the task to perform. It displays the options, reads the choice with a Scanner method, and a switch statement (or an if-else-if ladder) runs the matching task. The other options describe things that have nothing to do with the choice of the user.
